Methodology — how every FLUX number is made

The LLM cost-saving market has a measurement problem, documented by independent work rather than by us: three popular open-source token trimmers claiming 60–90% savings delivered 3.7% when independently replayed over 614M tokens of real traffic; a prompt-slimming technique modelled at ~77% measured ~13% in production. The gap comes from measuring per *request* instead of per *completed task*, and from ignoring provider cache economics. FLUX's method exists to be immune to both.

The rules every published number passes

1. Per completed task, not per request. A technique that shrinks each prompt but multiplies round trips has saved nothing. Our harness runs multi-turn tasks end to end and prices the whole task. 2. Quality held, measured. A claimed arm must keep at least 36 of 40 tasks fully correct and complete. A changed tool call is a hard failure; a shortened answer is scored by degree. The simulated model's quality signal punishes trimming recent context — the fixture is built to catch our own levers failing. 3. Provider cache rules simulated faithfully: minimum cacheable prefix, longest-exact-prefix matching, hit granularity, time-to-live expiry, and write premiums. Our simulator can and does show caching as a net loss on unfavourable traffic — that case has a unit test. 4. The provider's existing contribution is never claimed. On busy agent traffic, the provider's cache alone saves 35–40% before FLUX does anything. That figure is printed separately and excluded from every FLUX claim. 5. Tier savings are billed at the tier actually served. Discounted-tier requests can be bounced back to full price under load; the published async figure (57.7%) is net of assumed fallback rates, and per-request billing reads the service tier from the provider's response, not from our request. 6. Lossy levers pass a replay gate first. Changes that could affect answers (description trimming, output caps, tool-result capping) are enabled only after replaying your recorded requests both ways, with statistics corrected for having searched multiple configurations. The gate has rejected our own levers — those rejections are documented, not tuned away. 7. Unpriced means excluded, never zero. A model or billing date the price catalogue cannot price is excluded from baselines and invoices, with the reason stated. Our catalogue is dated and source-linked; a price change never silently reprices history. 8. The invoice is recomputable. Every request emits an append-only, hash-chained event carrying provider-verbatim usage, the catalogue version, levers applied, and gate verdict references. recomputeInvoice(events) is a pure function: run it yourself and you must get our number.

What "simulator-measured" means — and what it does not

All current figures come from a 40-task × 5-turn agent harness (plus one-shot variants) with realistic multi-kilobyte tool results, verified by an independent checker agent reproducing every number from command output, under 341 unit tests and 27 regression gates. They are honest measurements of the simulation. They are not yet measurements of your traffic — the pilot exists to produce that number, on your machine, from your logs, before you pay anything.

Known open items we publish rather than hide: per-model cacheable minimums are not yet in the simulator (the sparse-traffic 34.3% may overstate on some models); Anthropic batch rates are not yet catalogued (the async figure is OpenAI-priced); both are tracked in evidence.

flux — spend tokens where they matter. Every number on this site traces to a command and a commit — evidence. Savings are measured per completed task; estimates are always labelled. Source · llms.txt
